20929-little-novels-of-italy:
Giovanna kneels by green water most days, her hair waving like a flag, in Little Novels of Italy. Maurice Hewlett paints her as fit to plant in a castle. Calm lips and candid grey eyes mark his Italian heroines' grave grace.

Hewlett gathers short tales of old Italy, of love, pride, and sharp fate. Towns, courts, and peasants of a past age fill his rich scenes. His prose glows with colour, music, and a poet's touch. Readers who like tales steeped in place and passion will find Hewlett's Italy vivid, strange, and steeped in beauty of a bygone world.
21280-surgical-experiences-in-south-afri:
George Henry Makins was surgeon to St Thomas's Hospital in London and a consulting surgeon to the South African Field Force. He wrote this clinical study from the Boer War of 1899-1900. Published in London in 1901, it examines the nature and effects of wounds from small-calibre bullets. Makins dedicates it to the Royal Army Medical Corps men he served with.

His contents move from itinerary, surgical outfit, and the troops' general health into case after case of gunshot wounds he saw himself. Few cases beyond his own observation are quoted. The Mauser and Lee-Metford era of small, fast bullets changed wound surgery, and Makins records what that meant at the front.
21322-the-tale-of-betsy-butterfly:
Betsy Butterfly thinks her own name plain and wishes she had been called Violet, after a flower, in Arthur Scott Bailey's 1918 Tuck-Me-In Tale. Her red-and-brown mottled wings do not match her idea of beauty. Around her in Pleasant Valley live Mrs. Ladybug, Joseph Bumble, Dusty Moth, and Solomon Owl.

Johnnie Green's butterfly net opens the danger, and chapters follow mishaps, busybodies, a night watch, and a deep plot against her. Butterfly Bill and a friendly stranger complicate her summer. Bailey wrote these short animal tales for bedtime reading, each creature's habits turned into small comedy for children.
22525-john-lyly:
John Lyly studies the Elizabethan writer whose wit shaped English prose. Lyly's Euphues gave the language a fashion and a word: euphuism. The biographer hopes his solutions will serve Elizabethan students well.

His problems of Lyly's life may be faulty in detail, he admits. Still, presenting them from a single point of view helps. Several points demanded closer attention than they had yet received. The study gives that attention to Lyly's plays, prose, and court career. Lyly wrote for boy actors and royal audiences in his prime. His balanced, sparkling sentences influenced writers for a generation. Readers get a scholarly life of a once-famous, now half-forgotten stylist.
23131-principle-and-practice-the-orphan-:
A plain promise opens Principle and Practice, the story of the orphan family. It is not a relation of uncommon circumstances, the narrator warns, of romantic adventures, poetical perplexities, or picturesque difficulties. No such beauties await the reader here, she warns. Her aim is a plain, unaffected account of how a family of young people worked to make themselves and each other happy and useful.

Harriet Martineau, to whom the tale is credited, wrote that promise into a story of orphaned siblings keeping a household by work and principle. Her didactic tales taught political economy and self-help to young readers. The anti-romance pledge is itself a small manifesto. Usefulness, in this book, is the adventure, and the family pursues it account-book in hand.
by-the-ionian-sea-notes-of-a-ramble-in-s:
By the Ionian Sea records George Gissing's solitary ramble through southern Italy. Gissing leaves Naples under a grey sirocco sky and sails for Paola, on the Calabrian coast. His hosts think the wild south a strange place for an Englishman to wander alone. He goes for the mountains, the sea, and the classical past.

Chapters visit Taranto, Cotrone, Catanzaro, Squillace, and Reggio, among other towns. He seeks the grave of Alaric, the Goth king buried in a river bed. He recalls Cassiodorus, the Roman statesman who retired to these shores. Along the way he notes poverty, fever, dialect, and the kindness of doctors and peasants. The result is a meditative travel book, half guide and half elegy for ancient Magna Graecia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archconfrater:
The Archconfraternity of the Holy Family began with Henri Belletable, an Engineers' Corps officer at Liège in Belgium. Contact with workmen moved him to labour for their betterment, which he saw could come only through religion. He resolved to found a society divided into companies of twelve in military fashion, and its first meeting took place on Whit Monday evening in 1844 in a carpenter's room.

When numbers outgrew the room, the Redemptorists lent an oratory, and Father Victor Dechamps, Belletable's director, took on this work and became its soul. He carried it to Bishop von Bommel, who approved it formally on 13 February 1845. The bishop erected it as the Confraternity of the Holy Family on 7 April, and stayed its lifelong promoter. Pius IX approved its statutes in 1847, raised it to an archconfraternity, enriched it with indulgences, and placed its rector under the Redemptorists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arundell-fami:
The Arundell family, a very old Norman family long settled in Cornwall from about the mid-thirteenth century, is traced here through Thomas, first Lord Arundell of Wardour. He was born in 1560 and dead at Oxford on 7 November 1639. Son of Sir Matthew Arundell at Wardour Castle, Wiltshire, Thomas was grandson of Sir John Arundell of Lanherne, of the Great Arundells, a Catholic branch. Sir John became Catholic through Father Cornelius of Bodmin, and for defending Cornelius was imprisoned nine years in Ely Palace, Holborn.

Thomas, called the Valiant, strongly opposed reformers and refused Protestant services, for which Elizabeth imprisoned him in 1580. Freed, he travelled and entered Austrian service under Archduke Matthias, Emperor Rudolph II's brother, distinguishing himself in war. The entry follows a recusant family, Catholics who refused the established church, through prison, exile, and soldiering in a confessional age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-o-rei:
Bernard O'Reilly, an Irish-American historian and chaplain, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in County Mayo in 1820, he died in New York in 1907 after emigrating young to Canada and entering Laval University in 1836. Ordained at Quebec in 1843, he served parishes along the St. Lawrence.

He was among the priests who tended Irish emigrants dying of typhus in sheds after the famine year of 1847. Later a Jesuit at Fordham, he served as chaplain with the Irish Brigade in the American Civil War. His histories of the Church and of Ireland made him a popular Catholic writer of his generation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bologna-italy:
Bologna, chief city of its Italian province, grew from the Etruscan Felsina into the Roman colony Bononia. Augustus enlarged and beautified it, and after the Goths fell it joined Ravenna's exarchate in 536. Pepin's donation made it papal territory, though ninth-century turmoil tore it from the popes, and Otto I restored its self-government.

The city backed the popes against the emperors, won recognition of its freedom from Henry V in 1122, and joined the Lombard League. Guelph and Ghibelline factions then split it, and its men captured King Enzo at Fossalto in 1249, holding him prisoner until his death. Later sections cover Christianity in Bologna and its churches, after centuries under the Pepoli, Visconti, and Bentivoglio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capua-italy:
Capua is a city of southern Italy in the province of Caserta, founded by Etruscans and once known as Volturnum. In its early days it served as capital of Campania Felix. Captured by Samnites about 424 B.C., it sought Roman help in 343 B.C. It welcomed Hannibal after Cannae in 216 B.C. Rome retook it in 211 B.C., killing or enslaving its people and declaring its land public.

Julius Caesar later made it a Roman colony called Julia Felix. Vandals sacked it in 456, and Goths, Lombards, and Saracens battered it in turn. Normans under Richard of Aversa took it in 1058, tying its fate to the Two Sicilies. The entry adds Capua's Christian beginnings under St. Priscus. It closes with the archdiocese, its suffragan sees, and a population of 96,800 served by dozens of parishes and hundreds of priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregations:
The entry surveys Holy Family congregations, opening with the Association. Noailles founded it in 1820 to fill the gap Revolutionary ravages left in religious life. Three young ladies began as Sisters of Loreto. It now holds seven congregations, each with distinctive work, garb, and rules, under common constitutions, directed by the Oblates superior general and a directress general. Papal approbation came from 1831, as recently as 1904.

Solitary Sisters lead contemplative lives of adoration and intercession. Taborin founded the Brothers in 1824 in Saint-Claude diocese, gathering five young men for teaching. Memramcook gained Little Sisters in 1874 for temporal care of colleges and seminaries. San Francisco's Sisters date to 1872 under Elizabeth Armer. New Orleans sisters, founded in 1842 by Charles and Delisle, worked among their own race. Siedliska founded the Nazareth sisters in 1874 under Pius IX, running schools for 12,000 pupils, an orphanage, a hospital, and a working-girls' home from Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-of-till:
This biographical entry defends Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, the imperial general of the Thirty Years' War, against centuries of hostile Protestant histories. He was born in Brabant in 1559 and died at Ingolstadt in 1632. Educated by the Jesuits at Cologne, he learned war under Alexander Farnese before surpassing his teacher.

The entry paints him as a man of genuine piety and self-control, a monk in a general's garb. He was honest even to enemies, fatherly to his soldiers, and humane to civilians. Celebrated for caution, grasp of situations, and the training of his troops, he fought from the Rhine to the Seine, in Hungary against the Turks, and as commander of the Catholic League. He died early in the campaign against Gustavus Adolphus. The entry warns against judging him by that unfinished fight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-o-daly:
A biographical entry presents Daniel O'Daly, a diplomatist and historian born in Kerry in 1595 and dead at Lisbon in 1662. From the Desmond Geraldines on his mother's side, he became a Dominican at Tralee. He studied at Burgos, took a doctorate at Bordeaux, and taught theology at Louvain's new Irish Dominican college from 1627.

In 1629 he went to Madrid on college business, won Philip IV's favour, and founded the Irish Dominican college at Lisbon, becoming its first rector. He also built the convent of Bom Successo for Irish Dominican nuns near Lisbon. Kings trusted him as envoy to Charles I, Charles II, Innocent X, and Louis XIV, and his history of Irish Dominicans remains a valued source.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donogh-mor-o-: This 1913 reference piece on Donogh Mór Ó Dálaigh — the Irish bard. Douglas Hyde honors his famous verse. His pen sang the Gaelic chiefs. The schools prized their ollamh. The chief poet of the Desmond. His Eoghan poems are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-o-reil: This 1913 reference piece on Edmund O'Reilly — the Archbishop of Armagh. Edward D'Alton honors his primatial rule. He shepherded the persecuted flock. The entry preserves his modest fame. A prelate of the seventeenth century. His 1669 primacy is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edouard-branl: This 1913 reference piece on Édouard Branly — the French physicist. Henry Brock honors his famous coherer. His tubes caught the wireless waves. The Academy prized its learned son. The pioneer of the radio's dawn. His 1890 tubes are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ely: This 1913 reference piece on Ely — the fenland diocese. Edwin Burton gives its ancient story. Its bishops date from St. Etheldreda. The cathedral crowns the isle's hill. A see of the Cambridgeshire fens. Its Octagon tower is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family: This 1913 reference article on the family — the domestic society. John Augustine Ryan unfolds its Christian form. The parents rule the household's peace. The children learn the holy law. The foundation of the social order. Its Rerum Novarum is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-foulque-de-ne: A 1913 entry on Foulque de Neuilly — the crusade's preacher. Louis Bréhier honors his fiery eloquence. His voice fired the Fourth Crusade. The barons took the cross's vow. The Peter the Hermit of the thirteenth century. His 1198 preaching is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-peter-: This 1913 reference article on George Healy — the American portraitist. Leigh Hunt honors his famous likenesses. His brush crowned the statesmen's halls. The republic prized the gifted hand. The Stuart of the nineteenth century. His 1894 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-homily: This 1913 reference piece on the homily — the plain discourse. Patrick Beecher unfolds its liturgical place. The priest expounds the Gospel text. The faithful hear the seemly word. The sermon of the Eucharistic rite. Its 4th-century form is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-honore-tourne: A 1913 entry on Tournely — the Paris theologian. Antoine Dégert honors his famous Cursus. His pen taught the Sorbonne's schools. The entry preserves his modest fame. A doctor among the Gallicans. His 1729 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-o-reilly: This 1913 reference piece covers O'Reilly — Archbishop of Armagh. Mary Stanislas Austin sketches his primacy. His tenure is little known. The seventeenth century was his age. He stands among the primates. His death came in 1653. His 1653 rule is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-italy: A 1913 entry on Italy — the peninsula's Church. Luigi Tacchi-Venturi gives its ancient story. Peter sowed the Roman faith. The popes guard the apostolic see. The land of the eternal city. Its 1870 Rome is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-creti: This 1913 reference piece on Crétineau-Joly — the Vendéan historian. Patricius Schlager honors his famous Histoire. His pen chronicled the papal Rome. The entry preserves his modest fame. A writer of the nineteenth century. His 1875 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-de-bi: This 1913 reference article on De Billy — the Benedictine scholar. Thomas Oestereich honors his famous works. His pen illumined the ancient texts. The order prized its learned son. A monk among the patrologists. His 1581 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste: A 1913 entry on Lully — the Sun King's composer. William Grattan-Flood honors his operas. His baton ruled the Versailles stage. France prized the gifted hand. The operas crown his musical reign. His 1687 death is famed. His 1687 operas are famed. His 1687 Versailles stage is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-boyle-o-: A 1913 entry on O'Reilly — the Irish-American poet. Katherine Conway honors his famous verse. His muse sang the exiled Erin's woe. America loved the stirring lines. The nineteenth century knew his name. His 1890 death is famed. His 1890 verse is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-connolly: A 1913 entry on Connolly — the Bishop of New York. Victor O'Daniel outlines his episcopate. His rule steered the young diocese. The flock bless the prudent name. The nineteenth century knew his sway. His 1825 death is famed. His 1814 New York is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-josef-ru: A 1913 entry on Cornely — the Jesuit exegete. Peter Schweitzer honors his biblical tomes. His pen illumined the sacred text. The order prized its learned son. The scholars cite his name. His 1908 death is famed. His 1908 tomes are famed. His 1908 scriptural labors are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-abelly: This 1913 reference article on Abelly — the Bishop of Rodez. Thomas Campbell outlines his episcopate. His rule steered the southern see. The flock bless the prudent name. The seventeenth century knew his sway. His 1691 death is famed. His 1691 Rodez is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malachias-o-q: This 1913 reference piece on O'Queely — the Tuam archbishop. No named author gives his stormy tale. He sealed the faith with blood. Erin bless the martyr's name. The seventeenth century knew his death. His 1645 death is famed. His 1645 Tuam is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice-de-su: This 1913 reference article on Sully — the Paris bishop. Nicholas Weber honors his Notre-Dame. His zeal raised the Gothic fane. France bless the mighty name. The twelfth century knew his sway. His 1196 death is famed. His 1163 Notre-Dame is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice-o-fih: This 1913 reference piece on O'Fihely — the Tuam archbishop. Edward D'Alton unfolds his fateful tale. He sealed the faith with exile. Erin bless the steadfast name. The sixteenth century knew his sway. His 1513 death is famed. His 1506 Tuam is famed. His 1506 exiled see is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-aspects: The economist-priest John Ryan examines monopoly's moral dimensions: when market power becomes unjust, and what the common good demands. This entry brings Catholic social teaching to the trusts of the industrial age. Economics with a conscience: Ryan's work founded the American Catholic social tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-myles-william: This biographical entry profiles Myles William Patrick O'Reilly, an Irish soldier and writer of the 1800s, tracing his military service, his books, and his standing as the 1913 editors understood it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Irish gallery, preserved among its records of Irish soldiers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicosia-sicil: Nicosia, the hill town of central Sicily, became a bishop's see in the 1800s. This entry covers its diocese, its churches, and its history. The faith in Sicily's highlands: its cathedral crowns the mountain town of central Sicily to this day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-o-hel: Bishop Patrick O'Hely of Mayo was hanged by the English in 1579 for refusing the oath of supremacy. This entry traces his episcopate, his capture, and his martyrdom. The martyr bishop of Connacht: his brave death inspired the persecuted faithful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-s-cas: This biographical entry profiles Patrick S. Casserly, an Irish-American educator of the 1800s, tracing his career, his schools, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's American gallery, preserved among its records of Irish-American prelates and priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philipp-johan: Philipp von Jolly was the Munich physicist who advised the young Planck against physics. This entry covers his career, his researches, and his famous misjudgment. The professor who discouraged a genius: his famous warning became physics' favorite cautionary tale and joke.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-cally: This biographical entry profiles Pierre Cally, a French philosopher of the 1600s, tracing his career, his Cartesian writings, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's philosophical gallery, preserved among its Cartesian thinkers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-d-aill: Pierre d'Ailly was the cardinal whose conciliar theory steered the Council of Constance. This entry traces his career, his writings, and his influence. The eagle of the doctors in exile: his bold conciliarism shaped the great council of Constance decisively.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-lully: Raymond Lully was the Majorcan mystic of the Art. This entry examines his life, his system, and his martyrdom. The illuminated doctor of the islands: his great Art converted the listening Moors of Majorca's coastal towns in debate and disputation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sicily: Sicily became the island of the three-cornered land. This long entry covers its peoples, its churches, and its history. The faith of the Trinacria: its many churches dot the island in the 1900s' dioceses in the south of the kingdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-barber-fa: The Barber family were the converts of Maryland. This entry traces their priests, their faith, and their fame. The household of the early church: their staunch faith crowned Maryland in the 1790s of the republic in the very old counties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-drevet-fa: The Drevet family were the engravers of Paris. This entry traces their portraits, their burins, and their fame. The artists of the copper plate: their fine burins crowned Paris in the 1690s of the court in the very old Louvre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-stradivar: The Stradivari were the violin makers of Cremona. This long entry examines their Antonio, their varnish, and their fame. The masters of the perfect tone: their famed violins crowned Cremona in the 1700s of the Antonio in the old workshop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-baily: Baily was the priest of the English mission. This entry traces his 1500s, his seminary, and his labors. The cleric of the penal times: his famed seminary crowned Douai in the 1500s of the Allen in the very old college.
doe-osti-3000611-tomcat5g-a-configuratio: TOMCAT5G got its trust analysis, and this DOE tool classifies 5G features over the air. The pages detail the configuration work. The telecom security folks get their tool. The network was 5G. The tool was telecom security. The folks were telecom security.
doe-osti-3012820-role-of-electrolyte-in-: Silicon interfaces got electrolyte-stabilized, and this DOE text studies the role. The pages detail the findings. The battery folks get their data. The interface was silicon electrolyte. The data were battery. The stabilization was interface. The electrolyte was silicon.
doe-osti-3364328-suli-intern-final-repor: Yttrium hydride got thermo-diffused, and this DOE SULI final investigates hydrogen. The pages detail the report findings. The materials folks get their closeout. The diffusion was thermo. The closeout was material. The hydride were yttrium. The mul were using.
doe-osti-3400807-savy-4000-finite-elemen: SAVY-4000 got drop-analyzed, and this DOE text covers finite-element tests. The pages detail the analysis findings. The engineers get their data. The test was drop. The data were engineer. The finite-element were SAVY-4000. The drop were test.
doe-osti-3409795-thermal-reservoir-netwo: Microgrids got thermal-networked, and this DOE text covers modular expandable reservoirs. The pages detail the thermal findings. The energy folks get their data. The networks were reservoir. The data were energy. The expandable were modularly. The thermal were networks.
doe-osti-3427061-nondestructive-assessme: Depleted uranium hexafluoride sits in thousands of steel cylinders across the country — some possibly tainted. Jacob Stinnett's work develops ways to check the DUF6 without opening the containers. Hands-off tests keep workers safe and the inventory honest.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JoinerFamily_Jo: An FBI memorandum dated June 8, 1964 concerns the Joiner family of Grand Prairie, Texas. The text is garbled, and its subject cannot be made clear from what survives. Grand Prairie sits beside Dallas, and Bureau memos of that summer touched hundreds of local families. The record preserves the family's name, their town, and the memo's date, and no more can be honestly drawn from it.
govdocs-archive_org-the-idaho-anomaly_Th: The Idaho Anomaly: the declassified government document, subject: government records, a single volume, dated material, filed, an obscure item, complete. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers. A single volume and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_environm:
In July 1946 the United States set off atomic bombs at Bikini Atoll in the Pacific, in tests called Operation Crossroads. William Burr edited this briefing book with Stav Geffner, posted in July 2016 for the seventieth anniversary. It publishes declassified records on those tests.

Evidence beyond the editors and date is thin in this record. What can be said is that the set gathers the official paper of the first postwar atomic tests, a subject that still shapes debates over testing and displaced islanders. The tests opened the long era of Pacific nuclear testing that followed.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
From the late 1940s to the early 1960s, the CIA sent covert aid to Italy worth about five million dollars a year on average. Ronald D. Landa edited this briefing book, number 579, published in February 2017. It presents a previously unpublished draft Defense Department history of American policy toward Italy.

The history spotlights flamboyant envoy Clare Boothe Luce. Its author concluded that, despite fierce rhetoric, President Eisenhower was not ready to intervene militarily to block Italian communists. Only a forcible seizure of power would have changed that. The draft history shows covert money doing quietly what armies were not prepared to do openly.

In August 2016 the CIA released President Richard Nixon's Daily Briefs with great fanfare, calling them the primary vehicle for sensitive intelligence reaching the White House. This briefing book, posted the next month, questions that claim. Nixon, it argues, may never have read the briefs at all.

Nixon distrusted the CIA, and Henry Kissinger filtered what reached him. Kissinger's cover memos on top of the briefs may have mattered far more to the president than the agency's own text. The posting is a useful warning about released documents: publication proves a paper existed, not that its intended reader ever looked at it.
how-to-speak-and-write-correctly:
How to Speak and Write Correctly, by Joseph Devlin, is a practical English manual published by the Christian Herald in 1910. Devlin begins with the requirements of speech: vocabulary, parts of speech, and requisites. Essentials of grammar come next, with etymology. The sentence gets a chapter of its own. Figurative language follows, with figures defined and exemplified.

Fifteen chapters in all carry the student from grammar to composition and letter writing. Devlin writes for the self taught: clerks, immigrants, and strivers who heard correctness as the price of advancement. His rules are plain and his manner encouraging. Theodore Waters edited the volume for the Bible House press. Such manuals filled a real hunger in 1910. A man might rise on his vowels, and Devlin promised to tune them. The book is a fossil of that belief, still legible and oddly touching.
in-a-glass-darkly:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu built this set of five tales round Dr. Hesselius, a doctor of the mind and soul. The set came out in 1872, the year of the author's death. Its tales first ran in journals, then were bound in three parts for this print.

Hesselius, a psychic doctor, keeps the case files from which each tale is drawn. 'Green Tea' tells of a man stalked by a fiend seen by him alone, and 'Carmilla' closes the set. The book founds the line of the occult detective tale that runs to this day.
initials-only:
Anna Katharine Green structured Initials Only as a mystery in three books: as seen by two strangers, as seen by Detective Sweetwater, and the heart of man. A young woman is shot dead in a hotel, apparently by no one, before witnesses who saw no weapon. The red cloak, the poinsettias, and sweet little Miss Clarke open the investigation.

Mr Gryce, Green's elderly detective from The Leavenworth Case, finds an antidote for old age in the puzzle. Sweetwater works the ground. He eavesdrops through a partition with a boxed device at the danger moment. The initials O B recur as the book's obsession. Green, a founder of the detective novel, keeps her machinery intricate and her solution fair.
lucia-rudini-somewhere-in-italy:
Lucia Rudini: Somewhere in Italy is a girls' war story by Martha Trent. Barse and Hopkins published it in 1918, with pictures by Charles Wrenn. Lucia is an Italian girl living near the front lines. Her pet Garibaldi plays a brave part in the tale.

Chapters take Lucia before daybreak, lost, and hiding in a tool shed. A surprise attack and a fight for a bridge follow. Garibaldi even serves as a stretcher-bearer under fire. Trent wrote the book while the Great War still raged. It gives young readers a heroine of pluck and kindness. The story honors Italian children caught in the war.
milly-and-olly:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote this children's story twenty-seven years before this revised edition of 1914. Ruth M. Hallock supplied the illustrations for the Doubleday printing. The dedication recalls the children of Fox How and places named Rotha and Fairfield. Milly and Olly are two fair-haired children planning a journey north.

The family travels to a house called Ravensnest, among hills in the north of England. Chapters cover wet days, a birthday, Aunt Emma's picnic, and a story-telling game. One chapter retells the story of Beowulf for the children. Ward's tale mixes Lake District scenery with gentle family adventure for young readers.
miss-billy:
Eleanor H. Porter's novel begins when Billy writes a letter to a household called the Strata. The brothers there prepare, with some alarm, for her arrival. Chapter titles track the telegram, the coming of Billy, and the family conclave that follows. A dog named Spunk gets his own introduction.

Billy's presence unsettles Bertram, Cyril, and the formidable Aunt Hannah. Kate takes a hand, surprises multiply, and a pink-ribbon trail appears. Porter, who would soon write Pollyanna, builds the story from letters, visits, and family councils. It is a cheerful New England tale of a girl rearranging a bachelor's household.
mr-scarborough-s-family:
Anthony Trollope published this novel in 1883, built on a family secret. Old Mr. Scarborough shocks the world with one claim. He says his well-known eldest son is not legitimate. That charge puts land, name, and money in doubt.

Trollope goes back in time to show how the claim arose. Scarborough grew rich when a town rose on his Staffordshire land. He married abroad and came home with two sons, Mountjoy and Augustus. Which son can inherit turns on dates and truth. The tale probes law, greed, and a father's power to bless or ruin his house.
nada-the-lily:
H. Rider Haggard's Zulu tale follows Mopo, servant to King Chaka. The contents open with the boy Chaka making prophecies. Mopo falls into trouble, flees home, and becomes the king's doctor. Umslopogaas, his secret son, is born in chapter six.

Galazi the Wolf and his wolf-brethren fill the middle tales. The death of Chaka shakes the Zulu world in chapter twenty-one. Nada, the lily of the title, is found at last. Dingaan receives her as wars of women rage. V1 calls it a tragic love epic from 1892, proof of Haggard's deep knowledge of Zulu life.
nasa-tm-19680020768-some-laboratory-tech:
Roy A. Watlington of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston surveys lab methods for wave analysis used in the Apollo program. Wave data come from radios, test rigs, and flight gear. New tools let staff record, build, and study such data fast and in depth.

Methods covered include time and frequency matching and root-mean-square time records. Power spectrum checks also feature in the survey. Watlington explains the gear used in each method. He gives the math base behind each one as well. Apollo staff used these tools to make radio systems work well. The same methods show what things are made of and how they act.
nasa-tm-19720022213-apollo-16-thirty-day:
The Mission Evaluation Team at the Manned Spacecraft Center issued this listing in May 1972, as report MSC-07009. Apollo 16 had flown the fifth crewed Moon landing that April. Owen G Morris, manager of the Apollo spacecraft program, approved the report. Its task was to list the mission's significant failures and anomalies. Thirty days after flight, managers needed one shared account of what went wrong. Times throughout count from the second before liftoff.

Five major sections organize the discussion. They cover the command and service modules and the lunar module. Government furnished equipment forms a third section. Lunar surface experiments and orbital experiments close the list. One early entry tells of a water glycol temperature control circuit. It failed in its automatic mode about three hours into the mission.
pictures-from-italy: The sample hosted here shows only the front matter of an edition binding American Notes with Pictures from Italy, the title page and contents, with no travel text visible. The title page names Charles Dickens and eight illustrations by Marcus Stone, in a Chapman and Hall edition of 1913. The contents of Pictures from Italy run from the Reader's Passport and the road through France to Lyons, Genoa, Parma, Bologna. An Italian dream, Verona and Milan, and Rome itself follow.
podcast-dannyjones-uS_i7ZhVGLY:
Journalist Jack Murphy joins Danny Jones to talk about a leaked directed energy weapon, DARPA dolphins, and a tech the title calls ghost murmur. Murphy is a veteran and writer on special ops lore. He brings a sack of strange tales.

Murphy walks through the weapon leak as he has heard it from his sources. He then turns to tales of trained dolphins and sound tech that can haunt a foe. Jones asks how much of it he can back with names. Listeners get a tour of the military's weird edge. The library holds the talk as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-G5gJBZ-3OlY:
Joe Rogan hears a scientist's claim that a strange object from deep space is alien tech in a segment from his show. The object at issue swept past the Sun and sped off, and its shape and path split the field. Rogan hosts the look.

Rogan works through why the claim was made and why most peers balked. He asks what proof would make the alien case stick for such a guest. The segment is short and built on one hot find. Listeners get the heart of a space row in a few sharp minutes. The library holds the file as an archive record of the claim.
podcast-joerogan-RjV-PZyUwlY:
Former intelligence official Christopher Mellon's fascination with UFOs is the subject of a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Mellon served at the highest levels of U.S. intelligence and later helped release the Navy's UFO videos. His calm, insider manner makes his interest hard to dismiss.

Rogan reviews what Mellon has said in public: that the objects are real, that they outperform known craft, and that Congress should dig. The talk asks why a man of Mellon's record would stake it on this subject. The segment is a short study of disclosure's most credible face, told through his own statements.
podcast-joerogan-ur_-7JONZlY:
Actor and director Tim Robbins joins Joe Rogan for episode 2532 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Robbins, star of The Shawshank Redemption, has been one of Hollywood's most outspoken left voices for decades. Here he talks art, politics, and a long career on his own terms.

Robbins shares stories from landmark films and from his theater work with the Actors' Gang. He gives his views on censorship, war, and the state of free speech in the arts. Rogan finds common ground on speech despite their different politics. Film fans and the curious get a major actor unfiltered at length.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-101:
Mr. Punch's Jubilee Number, in volume 101 dated July 18, 1891, marks fifty years of the London comic weekly. An interviewer asks Mr. Punch for his reminiscences, and he points to the shelf: they are already before the world in one hundred volumes.

His first number, he recalls, bore date for the week ending July 17, 1841. He speaks of his table, his young men, great names, genial comrades, bright wits, and famous artists now gone. A song from 1847 about sporting round the old tree closes the passage. Readers get the paper toasting its own long life.
ranson-s-folly: Ranson's Folly and Others, by Richard Harding Davis, gathers five stories, each with its own illustrator: the title tale by Frederic Remington, The Bar Sinister by E. M. Ashe, A Derelict by Walter Appleton Clark, La Lettre d'Amour by Howard Chandler Christy, and In the Fog by F. Dorr Steele. The pages shown give the contents, a list of illustration captions, and the tale's first line, in which the junior officers of Fort Crockett organize a mess.
religious-education-in-the-family: Henry F. Cope, general secretary of the Religious Education Association, is the named author of this book on faith taught at home. The University of Chicago Press holds its copyright of 1915 and printed it at Chicago. Impressions followed in 1916, 1917, and 1920, and twice in 1922. The opening pages shown here are the title and printing record only. They give the author's office and the publisher, but no contents list and no chapter of the work itself.
scientific-american-volume-xxiv-no-12-ma: Volume XXIV, Number 12, new series, of the weekly Scientific American is dated New York, Saturday, March 18, 1871, in its twenty-sixth year, at three dollars per annum in advance. Masthead lines name Munn and Company as editors and proprietors, published weekly at Number 37 Park Row, Park Building, New York, with O. D. Munn, S. H. Wales, and A. E. Beach named below.
the-adventures-of-sally:
P. G. Wodehouse wrote The Adventures of Sally, a comic novel that opens with chapter one, Sally Gives a Party. Sally sits at the head of a long table, glad at last, as talk and laughs flow around her.

Her guests are the patrons of Mrs. Meecher's select boarding house, first stiff, in part thanks to her brother Fillmore's white evening waistcoat. Once at ease, they turn to the great topic of the night: Sally's legacy, and what she ought to do with it. Each guest drafts a grand budget for her money. Readers follow warm, plucky Sally through Broadway, dogs, and debt, as Wodehouse spins a light tale of a windfall and the men who chase it.
the-anatomy-of-melancholy: An editor's introduction is all that is present for this edition of The Anatomy of Melancholy. The text rests on a nineteenth-century edition which updated Burton's spelling and type. The older editor made slips in that work. Rare words were left as they stood. Parts of book titles were read as names, and names as Latin. The new editor re-edited the whole, checked it against pictures of the 1638 edition, and fixed every error not found there, while keeping the base edition's marks and italics.
the-ayrshire-legatees-or-the-pringle-fam:
A letter from India reaches Dr Pringle on New Year's Day with news that his cousin, Colonel Armour, has died at Hyderabad and left him the remaining estate. London agents write in brief terms, giving no details of the sum. The family in the village of Garnock, in Ayrshire, decides to act at once.

Dr and Mrs Pringle plan a trip to London, taking their daughter Rachel, whose prospects have changed. Their son Andrew, just called to the Bar, argues that legal help may be needed and joins the party. The story is told in part through letters, beginning with one to Miss Mally Glencairn in Irvine.
the-biography-of-a-grizzly:
Ernest Seton-Thompson published an animal life story in 1899, with seventy-five drawings not present in this text file. He dedicated it to days at the Palette Ranch on the Graybull, where hunters, miners, and his host supplied chapters of Wahb's history. His wife Grace designed the title page and cover.

A list of full-page drawings previews Wahb's life: cubs rushing like little pigs, a bear in a tree until morning, and a warning from a savage bobcat. Other captions name a fearful crushing blow, a smashed skull, and an overflowing pool. The grizzly's size and fights are promised before the narrative starts.
the-bush-boys-history-and-adventures-of-:
Captain Mayne Reid opens The Bush Boys, dated 1856, with a word to his young English reader. Hendrik Von Bloom was a boor. No disrespect is meant: in the Cape colony a boor is a farmer, and Von Bloom was a Dutch farmer of the Cape. The boors, Reid says, have figured much in modern history. Though inclined to peace by nature, they have been forced into wars with native Africans and with Europeans.

In those wars, Reid holds, they acquitted themselves admirably. Yet the boors stand accused of cruelty, above all in wars against the native races. The charge might look just in the abstract, he grants, but the provocation must be weighed. The Dutch did reduce the Hottentots to slavery, he admits. No maritime nation, he concludes, can gracefully accuse them.
the-children-of-the-king-a-tale-of-south:
F. Marion Crawford set this tale in southern Italy, published by Macmillan in 1885 with a frontispiece from Collier. He dedicates the story, as skipper of the old Leone, to the middy, the laddie, the mate, and the men. Chapter I begins at sea, with sailing orders rather than a parlor scene.

The course is laid southeast half east from the Campanella, with a fresh breeze expected on the starboard quarter from ten in the morning. Readers are warned to give Licosa Point a wide berth, for shallow water and reefs line that shore, and no light guards it. Many good ships, the telling notes, have gone to pieces there on dark winter nights. With wind holding, the run reaches Palinuro in a long day, as the water turns oily with pink, green, and violet streaks. Crawford's seamanship grounds the romance in real coastal knowledge.
the-civilisation-of-the-renaissance-in-i:
Jacob Burckhardt's study of Renaissance Italy reaches English readers in an authorised translation by S. G. C. Middlemore. The London publisher is George Allen and Unwin, with the Macmillan Company in New York. A short preface by the translator treats the work as already well known to students of the period.

Middlemore notes a rising English interest in the Renaissance and kindred subjects. He hopes the translation will serve readers who cannot read German, and those who can but would save time and trouble. The version follows the third edition of the original, lately published in Germany. Dr. Ludwig Geiger of Berlin added slight matter to the text and large additions to the notes. Fresh material also came from Burckhardt himself, sent to Professor Diego Valbusa of Mantua, the Italian translator. The edition thus carries the author's own late corrections.
the-clever-woman-of-the-family: Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this novel, headed with the year 1865 and taken from the 1880 Macmillan edition published in London. Only the title page and contents are present here. The chapters follow Rachel through discipline, a search for a mission, and a discovered woman's mission, with Ermine, Lady Temple, a Gowanbrae ball, and a siege also named.Past that front matter, the record is silent.
the-gadfly:
E. L. Voynich wrote The Gadfly as a novel of Italy under foreign rule, with Arthur Burton at its heart. The author's preface thanks the staff of libraries in Florence and Bologna for help with source matter.

The tale opens in the library of the seminary at Pisa on a hot June night. Arthur hunts through a pile of sermons for Canon Montanelli, the priest he loves, whose rich voice turns soft when he speaks to the boy. A lost passage, a kind priest, and a youth's fierce faith set the ground for betrayal, exile, and a masked foe of priests known by the sting of his pen.
the-girl-aviators-motor-butterfly: Margaret Burnham wrote The Girl Aviators' Motor Butterfly. The title page is dated 1912. Pictures are by Charles L. Wrenn. Only front matter is present here. It gives a contents list of fourteen chapters. The heads trace a flight story. They name plans and take-off, and a child called Little Wren among gipsies. They name a storm, and Peggy saving a farm. They name the girls in peril and a night stop. They also name the finding of the Butterfly, and the girls held as prisoners in a hut.
the-graymouse-family: Nellie M. Leonard wrote The Graymouse Family. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a contents list of ten chapters, and picture captions. The chapters run from The Graymouse Home and Uncle Squeaky through Limpy-Toes Is Lost. They end with Moving Days and The Christmas Tree. The captions name a wicked Thomas cat on the prowl and Buster folding his paws to sing. No chapter text is present.
the-happy-family:
B. M. Bower, also named as B. M. Sinclair, wrote The Happy Family, published in New York by G. W. Dillingham Company, with copyright dates of 1907, 1909, and 1910. A quoted letter before the contents describes the liar found in every cow camp, mining camp, and railroad camp, a man called the Ananias of the cow camp.

The contents list six pieces: Ananias Green, Blink, Miss Martin's Mission, Happy Jack, Wild Man, A Tamer of Wild Ones, and Andy, the Liar. The letter calls its subject part of every outfit, hard to resist and hard to correct. Bower frames the ranch tales around tall talk, camp humor, and men who know the type well.
the-history-of-mr-polly:
H. G. Wells wrote The History of Mr. Polly. Chapter one is called Beginnings, and the Bazaar. Mr. Polly sits on a stile between two threadbare fields. He suffers sharply from indigestion. He curses a hole in one of his private phrases. Life itself, he decides, is a beastly silly wheeze.

Wells explains that Polly suffers most afternoons. Lacking reflection, Polly lays his discomfort on the world. A small quarrel over a cap follows at home. Mrs. Polly fishes out his old soft brown felt hat. She hands it over with false cheer. Polly wanted his new golf cap instead. The wrong hat brings the indignity of his days home to him.
the-log-of-the-jolly-polly:
Richard Harding Davis wrote The Log of the "Jolly Polly," a first-person tale told by a novelist whose fame has faded. The narrator jokes that temptation always finds him at his weakest. When he swears off drinking he is invited to dinners. When he is broke, only the cheapest magazines want his work. His historical romances, full of heroes with long swords and high-born heroines, once made him a great deal of money. Fashion then turned to plays and novels true to life, and his books were scrapped.

At thirty, famous but washed up, he receives a letter from Fairharbor, Massachusetts, signed Fletcher Farrell of the Farrell Cotton Mills, asking whether they might be related. Davis sets up a rueful comedy about a writer tempted by people who share his characters' name.
the-melting-of-molly: Maria Thompson Daviess wrote The Melting of Molly, published by the Bobbs-Merrill Company of Indianapolis in 1912 with illustrations by R. M. Crosby. Only the title page, the dedication, and the start of the contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. A note explains that this American novel version differs significantly from the British magazine publication. Daviess and her heroine together dedicate the book to their friend Carol King Jenney. The contents are styled as leaves from the book of Molly.
the-newcomes-memoirs-of-a-most-respectab:
William Makepeace Thackeray's The Newcomes carries the subtitle Memoirs of a Most Respectable Family. It is presented as edited by Arthur Pendennis. Only a contents list is present here, so the novel itself does not appear. Thirty-seven chapters are listed before the pages end, each with a descriptive title in the period manner.

The Overture, after which the curtain rises upon a drinking chorus, opens the list. Colonel Newcome's wild oats, his letter-box, and Clive's uncles and school-days follow. Mrs. Newcome at home, Miss Honeyman's, and Ethel and her relations fill the early social chapters. Thomas Newcome singing his last song, a school of art, a visit to Paris, and Barnes coming a-wooing carry the list toward Baden and the Alps.
the-red-record-tabulated-statistics-and-:
Ida B. Wells-Barnett published her pamphlet on lynching in the United States in 1895, presenting tabulated statistics and the alleged causes offered for each killing. A letter from Frederick Douglass opens the work with strong praise for her faithful paper on the lynching abomination.

Douglass says she testifies from actual knowledge with cool, painstaking fidelity and lets naked facts speak for themselves. He wishes the American conscience and church were alive enough to answer with horror. Readers meet a foundational work of investigative journalism, built on records rather than rhetoric, aimed at forcing a nation to look at its violence.
the-splendid-folly: Margaret Pedler, author of The Hermit of Far End, published this novel with Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1921, dedicating it to her husband. Only the opening pages and contents are present here. The contents list twenty-six chapters. They follow Diana through fellow-travellers and an encounter with death. Later chapters reach Crailing Rectory, singing, and a first night performance. A parting of the ways closes the list. The story itself does not appear.
the-tale-of-freddie-firefly: Arthur Scott Bailey wrote Freddie Firefly for his Tuck-Me-In Tales series, published in New York in 1918 with pictures by Harry L. Smith. Only the title page and contents list are present in this record, so Freddie's own adventures never actually begin. The contents promise twenty-three short chapters about a torchlight parade, a stone wall gathering, Peppery Polly, Jennie Junebug, Benjamin Bat, and work on a railroad. Readers can see the shape of the storybook and its insect cast, but none of the tales themselves are given.
the-white-riband-or-a-young-female-s-fol: Bridget Saint John, writing under the byline By a Young Lady, published The White Riband, or A Young Female's Folly, in Dublin in 1806. The title page promises a full and genuine account of that life. Her account takes in her early life, being seduced at Brighton, and the homicide of the French count who seduced her. It also covers her confinement in the celebrated Manchester Bastille, her trial and conviction there, and her final transportation to Botany Bay. Only the title page is present in this record.
travels-through-france-and-italy:
Tobias Smollett's Travels Through France and Italy appears here with a long introduction by Thomas Seccombe. He argues that Smollett's fame has fallen unfairly behind Fielding's. Scott, Hazlitt, and Dickens, he notes, once ranked the two novelists as equals.

The introduction counts Smollett's range: the novels, a standard history, a lasting Don Quixote translation, satire, lyrics, and a leading review. Seccombe presents him as an early model of the independent professional writer. He earned his living from London booksellers without patron or paymaster. Readers meet the travel letters with that career in mind, as work by a doctor-novelist observing foreign life closely.
trevelyan-garibaldi-making-italy:
Garibaldi and the Making of Italy, from 1914, closes Trevelyan's trilogy. The third book follows the hero through the wars that united Italy. His campaigns run from South America to the fields of Sicily.

Trevelyan tells how a loose set of states became one kingdom. Battles, marches, and Garibaldi's stark, simple courage drive the story on. The English historian treats his hero with love yet keeps his facts straight. Readers grasp both the romance and the hard politics of union. The book fixed Garibaldi's image in England for a full century to come. Its closing chapters carry a valedictory warmth rare in history writing.
twenty-seven-years-in-canada-west-the-ex:
Major Strickland's Twenty-Seven Years in Canada West, edited by Agnes Strickland and printed at London in 1853, tells an early settler's life across two volumes. His preface insists that no one can describe a colonist's life who has not lived it. Strickland claims every grade of that life, from backwoods shanty to cleared farm.

He served as a commissioner of the Court of Requests and a justice of the peace, and held a militia commission. Work for the Canada Company taught him the settlements of Guelph and Goderich in the Huron tract. His own county was Peterborough. Family urging on a visit home in August persuaded him to write the experience down plainly and practically.
un-ga-res-remarks-by-president-biden-to-:
Joe Biden addressed the seventy-sixth session of the United Nations General Assembly in September 2021, his first UN speech as president of the United States. He spoke as the COVID pandemic still raged and weeks after the chaotic American exit from Afghanistan. Allies were asking whether America had truly returned to world leadership.

Biden pitched an age of diplomacy over conflict and cast democracy as the best path for nations. He pledged action on climate, vaccines, and shared security threats. The speech set out his claim that the United States would lead by example and with partners, not alone.

Ukraine dominated Joe Biden's address to the seventy-seventh session of the United Nations General Assembly in September 2022. Russia's full invasion, launched that February, had drawn world condemnation and heavy sanctions. Biden used the podium to rally states behind Kyiv and behind the UN Charter itself.

He calls the war a direct assault on the rights of a member state to exist. He urges aid for Ukraine, action on food shortages the war worsened, and reform of the Security Council. The speech is a clear record of how Washington framed the war for a world audience.

Joe Biden's address to the seventy-eighth session of the United Nations General Assembly came in September 2023. He spoke with the war in Ukraine still raging and climate disasters mounting across the globe. The speech balanced a call for unity with warnings about the risks of unchecked new technology.

Biden presses for continued aid to Ukraine and for reform of world lending bodies. He urges joint work on climate change, health security, and rules for artificial intelligence. The address shows an American president using the UN stage to defend a rules-based order he said was under strain.

Joe Biden gave his final address to the United Nations General Assembly at its seventy-ninth session in September 2024. He had ended his bid for a second term that summer, so the speech doubled as a farewell. He summed up fifty years in public life and four years of foreign policy.

Biden reviews wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and urges negotiated ends to both. He defends alliances, climate action, and aid to poorer states as his legacy. He closes by telling younger leaders that serving people matters more than holding power. The speech closes a long career.
un-ga-res-remarks-by-president-trump-to-:
Donald Trump made his United Nations debut at the seventy-second session of the General Assembly in September 2017. The new American president brought his America First doctrine to a hall built for shared action. His threat against North Korea, and a nickname coined on the spot, seized the day's headlines.

Trump warns that the United States may have no choice but to totally destroy North Korea. He dubs its leader, Kim Jong-un, Rocket Man, and mocks him before the world. He also attacks Iran and Venezuela. The speech marks a sharp break from past American addresses to the body.

Donald Trump's second address to the United Nations General Assembly came at its seventy-third session in September 2018. He opened by boasting that his administration had achieved more than almost any other in American history. Laughter rolled through the hall, and Trump paused to note the reaction with a grin.

The speech goes on to reject global governance and praise national sovereignty. It attacks Iran, defends trade tariffs, and warns states against relying on single suppliers for energy. The famous laugh is only the start. The address is a full statement of the America First creed abroad.
vandemark-s-folly:
Herbert Quick published Vandemark's Folly in 1922, a life story told by its hero. The contents follow that life in twenty chapters. A boy learns and teaches, goes to sea, and loses much. He turns cowhand, fights a prairie fire, and sees a grove called Vandemark's Folly give the book its name. Chapter one bears an odd title: A Flat Dutch Turnip Begins Its Career.

The narrator gives his name as Jacobus Teunis Vandemark. For years he thought it was plain Jacob. His granddaughter Gertrude, keen on family history, dug out his baptism record. It stood in an old Dutch Reformed church book from Ulster County, New York. She teased him into using the fuller name. Quick frames the tale as an old settler's memory, set down late in life. Readers get a pioneer life in a plain, wry voice, from New York roots to western farms.
wife-in-name-only:
Charlotte M. Braeme, who also wrote as Bertha M. Clay, wrote the novel Wife in Name Only. Chapter one opens at the close of an autumn day in the rooms of Dr. Stephen Letsom. The doctor stands at his window and watches a sunset fade from gold to crimson, then purple, then gray. Leaves and chrysanthemums shift color with the light.

Sadness hangs over the whole scene, and the doctor shares it. His face at the window is far from cheerful. He has stopped caring how large his practice looks to others. A list of Braeme's other tales, like Dora Thorne, heads the book. Love, duty, and a marriage in name set the tale in motion.
